problem_statement: The paper frames the task as dynamic portfolio optimization: finding the best investment trajectory for an investor at a chosen risk level, while also respecting a minimum holding period and integer-bundle constraints. It treats this as a real-life financial optimization problem in which the investor wants to maximize profit subject to risk and trading constraints.
problem_statement_quotes: Our aim is to find the best investment trajectory for an investor, given a level of risk that they want to take.
It is common for investors to impose a minimal holding period, preventing any purchased asset from being sold before a predetermined period of time.
classical_baseline: The paper compares against brute-force classical search and other classical solvers for portfolio optimization. It also references the standard Modern Portfolio Theory formulation as the underlying classical financial model.
classical_baseline_quotes: Compared to classical solvers, our method is way faster than brute-force classical search, which scales exponentially fast in the number of qubits and quickly hits astronomical numbers (the problem is clearly intractable in this sense for 50 assets).
Compared to other solvers, D-Wave quantum annealing is known to be faster and allow larger portfolios than solvers such as Gekko, see Table IV in Ref.29, which equally applies in our case.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the problem becomes hard classically because the discretization makes it a combinatorial optimization problem, and brute-force search scales exponentially and becomes intractable for large instances. It also says that enforcing the minimum holding period by a global penalty would make the problem even more computationally intractable because it would couple different time steps.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Compared to classical solvers, our method is way faster than brute-force classical search, which scales exponentially fast in the number of qubits and quickly hits astronomical numbers (the problem is clearly intractable in this sense for 50 assets).

Alternatively, we could include this constraint by penalizing in Eq. (3) trajectories which do not meet the minimum holding period. The corresponding penalty term would then correlate different time steps between each other, such that the cost function would not have the separable form of Eq. (4). In such a case, the problem would become even more computationally intractable, and a global optimization strategy over all possible trading times would be necessary from the very beginning.
business_stakes: The paper says the minimum holding period matters because short-term investments are taxed more heavily than long-term investments, and it notes that the timeframe is natural for realistic banking products. It also frames the work as relevant to commercial-value problems and financial products offered to investors.
business_stakes_quotes: An issue that investors often face is that short term investments tend to be taxed much higher than long term investments.
In this study, we imposed a minimal holding period of 7 days, which is a natural timeframe for some realistic banking products.
For problems of commercial value, this can be very large.
Moreover, we also show how our approach can easily produce trajectories adapted to different risk profiles, as typically offered in financial products.
extraction_notes: Clear motivation in abstract and introduction; classical difficulty is explicitly stated.
